title: Choose the quality of a lossy export and see what it will weigh
goal: Exporting a JPEG or a HEIC gives you whatever quality the app picked, with no way to change it and no idea how big the file will be until it is on disk. Let the quality be set, and show what the file will weigh at that setting while you are still deciding, so choosing between a sharp large file and a small good enough one is one slider and one number rather than exporting three times and looking in Finder.
notes:
Asked for by the user on 2026-09-15: "for formats which have variable qualities, i'd like to be able to adjust that and see the expected filesize."

BOTH HALVES ARE ALREADY PART BUILT, so this is mostly exposing what is there.
- Quality: Sources/PhotonzRender/ImageCodec.swift:33, encode(_:format:quality:) already takes a quality of 0 to 1, documented as applying to lossy formats and ignored by PNG, and passes it as kCGImageDestinationLossyCompressionQuality. Nothing in the dialog ever sets it, so every export goes out at the 0.9 default.
- The size line: Sources/Photonz/ExportDialog.swift already holds a byteCount state, and its comment says it is 'worked out only for a drawing made of shapes'. So the dialog already knows how to show what a file will weigh; it only does it for SVG.

THE ONLY HONEST WAY to know what a lossy file will weigh is to encode it and count the bytes. There is no formula worth trusting across pictures: a screenshot of flat UI and a photograph of leaves at the same quality differ by an order of magnitude. So encode to memory, in the background, and show the real number. That makes the performance note in the acceptance list the real work: a 12 megapixel document re-encoded on every tick of a slider will make the dialog crawl. Debounce it, do it off the main actor, show the last known number while a new one is being worked out, and say in the audit what was measured.

Do not let this grow into a general export rebuild. The scale row, the frame picker and the SVG handling in that dialog all work and are not part of this.

Related but separate, and NOT in this task: the user also asked for WebP export in the same message. That cannot be done the way these formats are done - ImageIO on macOS 26 cannot WRITE WebP, confirmed by CGImageDestinationCopyTypeIdentifiers which lists 22 writable types with no WebP among them - so it needs a bundled encoder and that is a decision about taking the project's first third party dependency. The user decided on 2026-09-15: bundle libwebp, WebP and not AVIF. It is filed as 'export-as-webp'. WebP is a lossy format (and a lossless one), so it joins this task's rule the moment it exists; whichever of the two lands second follows the first rather than inventing a second quality control.
acceptance: Exporting a format that has a quality offers one, and the control is absent rather than dead for a format that does not
The size the dialog shows is what the saved file actually weighs, checked by saving and comparing the bytes, not an estimate from a formula
The number keeps up while the quality is being changed, without the dialog stuttering: say in the audit how long a 12 megapixel document takes to weigh and what was done about it
Changing the scale changes the number too, since 2x is a different file
The quality you chose is remembered for next time, per format, so somebody who always wants eighty percent sets it once
What a quality setting costs is visible, not just its size: the audit shows the same picture at the extremes so the tradeoff is real rather than abstract
A quality that would produce something visibly broken is not reachable by accident, or the audit argues why the full range is right
PNG and SVG are unaffected: neither grows a control that means nothing for it
Audit under queue/audits/ with the dialog at several qualities and the saved sizes beside the shown ones, and anything rough filed as a follow-up

log.note: user chose libwebp over AVIF; WebP filed as export-as-webp and joins this task rule

adversarial review before building. (1) A first-time user opens Export, picks JPEG and sees a slider at 90% and a size. The number answers 'how big', it does not answer 'how bad'. The full answer is a side-by-side preview of the artifacts, which needs a picture surface a 320pt sheet does not have and is a much bigger feature; the short version is a plain word beside the percentage (Best/High/Good/Low/Rough) plus a floor that keeps the reachable range usable. Building the preview is noted as rough, not built. (2) There is no mock for this, so nothing to disagree with; the shape is taken from what the sheet already does for SVG (a line under the format row saying what the file will be and what it will weigh). (3) Cut: a PNG size readout. It would be genuinely useful when choosing between PNG and JPEG, but PNG compression of a 12MP composite is much slower than JPEG and the sheet opens on PNG by default, so every Export would pay for a number nobody asked for. Noted as rough. (4) Shortest version that delivers the value: one slider, one exact byte count, remembered per format. That is what gets built. (5) Collision check: with frames on, the destination picker on and the format row, the sheet is already tall; quality adds two rows and only for JPEG and HEIC. (6) The real risk is cost. The render does not depend on the quality at all, only on the frame and the scale, so the render is kept and only the encode repeats as the slider moves, and the whole thing runs off the main actor behind a debounce. (7) HEIC at 80 and JPEG at 80 are not the same picture, which is why the memory is per format rather than one number.

left rough, not filed: (a) a preview of what a quality costs, inside the sheet. A person WILL want it, but it is a much bigger feature than this task and the audit's evaluate list asks the user directly whether the number alone is enough, so their answer becomes the task rather than my guess. (b) a size readout for PNG, cut on purpose for cost, also asked in the audit. (c) HEIC at 60 and JPEG at 60 are not the same picture and the sheet does not say so; the size line is the only thing that tells you, and it tells you honestly. None of these is broken, so none of them earned a task. Folded into existing tasks instead: the no-picture-of-the-app problem into an-audit-gets-a-real-picture-of-the-app-again, and how WebP inherits this control into export-as-webp.

Export offers a Quality slider for JPEG and HEIC and says exactly what the file will weigh at it, by really encoding the picture rather than estimating. New: PhotonzCore/ExportQuality.swift (the rules: 30-100 in fives, the plain word, one remembered number per format, how to say a size), PhotonzRender/ExportSizer.swift (an actor that renders and encodes off the main actor and keeps the render, so only the encode repeats as the slider moves), PhotonzDocument.exportTarget(frameID:) (one answer to what Export is writing, so what is weighed and what is saved cannot differ), the row and the per-format memory in ExportDialog.swift behind next-export-quality (on by default in Next). Verified: swift build clean with and without PHOTONZ_PLAYTEST, Scripts/test.sh green (7127 tests, 570 suites) including a render test that writes the file and asserts the bytes on disk equal the shown number; artifacts produced through the app's own encoder on a real 1800x1400 screenshot (191 KB at 30%, 369 KB at 60%, 1.3 MB at 100%, 3.6 MB at 100%/2x, each written and weighed). 12 MP timing: 65-173 ms first weigh, ~11 ms per quality after. NOT verified: no walk ran, the Mac's screen was locked for the whole task, so Scripts/playtest/export-quality-walk.json has never executed and the audit ships no picture of the Export sheet and says so; a sweep is requested. Audit: queue/audits/2026-09-15-export-quality.json
